title: How Do VOCs Affect Indoor Air Quality?
h1: How Do VOCs Affect Indoor Air Quality in Your Home?
description: VOCs are chemicals that off-gas from paint, furniture and cleaners. Learn how they affect indoor air quality and your health, and how to cut them at home.
quick_answer: VOCs, or volatile organic compounds, are chemicals that evaporate from everyday products like paint, cleaners, furniture, flooring and air fresheners. Indoors they build up to higher levels than outside and can cause headaches, eye and throat irritation, and other health effects. Reducing sources and bringing in fresh air are the most effective fixes.
body:
What are VOCs?

Volatile organic compounds are a large group of carbon-based chemicals that turn into gas at room temperature. You've smelled them, from fresh paint, a new couch or a strong cleaning spray. Some VOCs have no smell at all.

Because homes are fairly closed spaces, VOCs released indoors tend to build up. Indoor levels are commonly higher than outdoor levels, and they can spike after a project like painting or installing new floors.

Where do VOCs come from in a home?

  • Paint, stains, varnishes and adhesives
  • New furniture, cabinets and flooring, especially pressed-wood products
  • Cleaning products, disinfectants and air fresheners
  • Personal care products such as hairspray, nail polish and perfumes
  • Candles, incense and fireplaces
  • Stored fuels, solvents and pesticides, often in an attached garage
  • Dry-cleaned clothes and some hobby supplies
  • Cooking, especially on a gas range

How do VOCs affect your health?

Effects depend on the specific chemical, how much is in the air and how long you're exposed. Short-term exposure can cause:

  • Headaches and dizziness
  • Eye, nose and throat irritation
  • Nausea or fatigue
  • Worsening of asthma symptoms

Some VOCs, such as formaldehyde and benzene, are linked to more serious long-term health effects at higher exposures. Children, older adults and people with asthma or chemical sensitivities tend to be more affected. If you have ongoing symptoms you think are related to your home, talk with a doctor.

How can I tell if VOC levels are high?

Strong chemical or "new" smells are the most obvious sign, but not every VOC has an odor. Many home air quality monitors include a VOC sensor. They don't tell you which chemical is present, but they show when total levels rise and fall, which helps you track down the source.

The garage deserves a close look. Many Southern California homes have the furnace or water heater in the garage alongside paint cans, gas cans and pool chemicals, and fumes can find their way inside through the door or leaky ducts.

Watch for spikes when you clean, cook, use personal care products or bring something new into the house. A reading that stays high all the time often points to a constant source, like new furniture or chemicals stored near living space.

How do I reduce VOCs in my home?

  1. Choose low-VOC or zero-VOC products for paint, adhesives and finishes.
  2. Air out new items. Unwrap furniture and mattresses in the garage or a well-ventilated room for a few days if you can.
  3. Ventilate during and after projects. Open windows and run exhaust fans while painting or cleaning, and for a while after.
  4. Store chemicals outside the living space. Keep paint, fuel and solvents sealed in the garage or a shed, and keep the door between the garage and house closed.
  5. Skip air fresheners and heavy fragrances. They often add VOCs rather than removing odors.
  6. Use the range hood when cooking, especially on a gas stove.
  7. Keep humidity and temperature moderate, since heat and moisture can increase off-gassing.

Can my HVAC system help with VOCs?

Standard filters catch particles, not gases, so a regular HVAC filter won't remove VOCs. What helps most is ventilation, bringing in fresh outdoor air when it's clean. That can be as simple as opening windows on mild days, which our coastal climate allows for much of the year, or adding mechanical ventilation that exchanges stale indoor air for fresh air.

The HVAC system can also work against you. Return ducts that leak in a garage can pull fumes from stored paint, fuel and car exhaust straight into the house. Sealing those leaks, and keeping the furnace closet or garage free of chemicals, removes a hidden source that's easy to overlook.

Activated carbon filters and some air purifiers can absorb certain VOCs, though their capacity is limited and they need regular replacement. Our indoor air quality team can look at your home's ventilation and filtration and recommend options that fit.
faqs: What are the most common VOCs in homes?
Common ones include formaldehyde from pressed-wood products and some fabrics, and chemicals from paints, cleaners, fragrances and fuels. Levels vary widely depending on what is in the home.
How long does it take for VOCs to go away after painting?
Most of the off-gassing happens in the first few days, but some can continue for weeks. Keep the space ventilated during and after painting, and use low-VOC paint to reduce it.
Only purifiers with a substantial activated carbon filter can absorb some VOCs, and the carbon needs replacing. HEPA filters alone don't remove gases. Ventilation and source control work better.
Does opening windows help with VOCs?
Yes. Fresh air dilutes indoor VOCs. Open windows when the outdoor air is clean, and keep them closed during wildfire smoke or high-pollution days.
